Pot
pŏt
n. (a vessel for boiling or storing; rendering Hebrew sir, tsintseneth, Greek stamnos)
From Anglo-Saxon pott. In Scripture the humblest vessel in the house becomes a memorial, a test of holiness, and a figure for the nation itself.

Biblical Definition

Pot is a common vessel that Scripture repeatedly loads with meaning. It is a memorial: “Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations” (Exo 16:33) — a kitchen jar set before God so that later generations would see what wilderness bread looked like. It is a measure of holiness: an earthen vessel in which a sin offering was boiled must be broken, but “if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water” (Lev 6:28) — porous things absorb what they contain, and some vessels cannot be cleansed, only destroyed. It is the emblem of the slavery men grow nostalgic for: Israel remembers “the flesh pots” of Egypt and wishes itself back (Exo 16:3). And Zechariah closes the canon's story of the pot by promising that every pot in Jerusalem shall be holiness unto the LORD — the whole distinction between sacred and common vessels finally abolished upward.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pot as a vessel more deep than broad, used for holding liquors and other things — and notes its many kinds, from the flesh-pot to the vessel of the potter.

expand to see more

POT, n. A vessel more deep than broad, made of earth, or iron or other metal, used for several domestic purposes.

2. A vessel of earth, or a cup, in which flowers are cultivated.

3. A measure of liquids; the quart of two pints.

To go to pot, to be destroyed, ruined, wasted or expended. A low phrase.

Key Scripture

Exo 16:33 — "And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein, and lay it up before the LORD, to be kept for your generations."

Lev 6:28 — "But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water."

Exo 16:3 — "And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger."

1Ki 7:45 — "And the pots, and the shovels, and the basons: and all these vessels, which Hiram made to king Solomon for the house of the LORD, were of bright brass."

Modern Corruption

The sacred and the ordinary severed, so that religion is confined to designated objects and hours — where Scripture moves in the opposite direction, making the cooking-pot holy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to correct is the sacred/secular split, which the pot refutes from both ends. A kitchen jar holds the manna before the LORD; the flesh pots of Egypt become the emblem of a heart that prefers slavery with meat to freedom with God; and a common cooking vessel is regulated by the law of the sin offering. Nothing in an Israelite household was outside the covenant, which is precisely what a modern believer forgets between Sunday and Monday.

Leviticus 6:28 rewards close reading. An earthen pot that has boiled a sin offering must be broken, because porous clay absorbs; a brasen one may be scoured and used again. The lesson is not that some sinners are disposable but that some vessels take in what passes through them. Habits, appetites, and company soak into a man, and there are things a person cannot merely rinse. The doctrine of mortification is written into the kitchen inventory.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sir (H5518), a pot, caldron — the flesh pots of Egypt; tsintseneth (H6803), the jar that held the manna; Greek stamnos (G4713), the golden pot of Heb 9:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew sir (H5518) — a pot, caldron; the flesh pots of Egypt (Exo 16:3) and the boiling pot of Jeremiah's vision (Jer 1:13).

Hebrew tsintseneth (H6803) — a receptacle, jar; used once, of the pot of manna laid up before the LORD (Exo 16:33).

Greek stamnos (G4713) — a jar; Hebrews calls it the golden pot that had manna, kept in the ark (Heb 9:4).

Usage

"“Take a pot, and put an omer full of manna therein” — a kitchen jar set before God."

"“The earthen vessel… shall be broken” — porous things absorb what they hold."

"“When we sat by the flesh pots” — nostalgia for slavery, remembered by its meat."
